summary: Michael Albada, a Principal Applied Scientist at Microsoft working on Security Copilot and its agents, presents a practical talk on building applications with AI agents, drawn from a forthcoming 300-page O'Reilly book with full code examples. He opens by noting strong industry momentum (254% increase in Y Combinator agentic startups over three years) but cautions that agentic benchmarks remain hard, with accuracy in the 50s–70s on complex multi-step tasks. He defines an agent as an entity that can reason, act, communicate, and adapt, treating the foundation model as a base augmented by components. He frames agency as a continuum (citing Andrew Ng) and adds a second axis—effectiveness—warning against building highly agentic but low-efficacy systems. Core components include tool use/function calling, orchestration patterns, and multi-agent systems. For tools, he strongly warns against one-to-one API-to-tool mapping and exposing too many tools in one prompt, which causes semantic collision and accuracy loss. For orchestration, he recommends starting simple with chains and trees, only moving to full agentic loops when chains become unwieldy. He advocates keeping fixed business logic deterministic and external to the model. Multi-agent systems are justified mainly to split large tool sets among semantically grouped agents coordinated by a router. He stresses investing heavily in evaluation, treating it as test-driven agent development: defining agents by expected inputs and outputs, building eval sets through human review, clustering failures, and moving from development by anecdote to batch-level analysis. He recommends open-source tools including Intel Agent (synthetic input generation), Microsoft's Pirate (red teaming/jailbreaking), Label Studio (evaluation set construction), and trace/textrad/dspI (automatic prompt optimization using a foundation model as judge). He then emphasizes observability—using open telemetry integrations, detailed logging, tracing, and automated clustering of failure modes—since generative models make production failures hard to understand. Common pitfalls include insufficient evaluation (the biggest), poor tool design (insufficient tools, unclear descriptions, semantic overlap), excessive complexity, and a weak learning loop. Coming from the cyber security division, he stresses that agentic systems are a new class of vulnerability: design for safety at every layer, install tripwires and detectors, and eject to human review in critical cases. He closes with a Paul Krugman quote on productivity, expressing optimism about an upshift in what individuals can accomplish.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agency is a spectrum, not binary; always prioritize effectiveness alongside agency to avoid low-value agentic systems.
Do not register APIs one-to-one as tools; too many tools per prompt causes semantic collision and accuracy degradation.
Start orchestration simple (chains, trees); move to agentic loops only when deterministic workflows become hard to maintain.
Keep fixed business logic deterministic and external to the model; use the agent only to update validated state.
Use multi-agent systems primarily to partition large tool sets into semantically grouped agents coordinated by a router.
Invest heavily in evaluation; adopt test-driven agent development with rigorous eval sets, batch analysis, and clustering of failures.
Move from development by anecdote to aggregate-level batch analysis for more intelligent optimization steps.
Leverage open-source eval and safety tools: Intel Agent, Pirate (red teaming), Label Studio, and automatic prompt optimization frameworks.
Prioritize observability with open telemetry, detailed tracing, and automated failure-mode clustering for production agents.
Design for safety at every layer: install tripwires, detectors, and human-review fallbacks for critical cases.

sections.title: Introduction and background
sections.summary: Michael Albada introduces himself as a Principal Applied Scientist at Microsoft, contributor to Security Copilot and its agents, formerly ML at Uber. The talk distills a forthcoming 300-page O'Reilly book with full code examples.

sections.title: Promise and obstacles of agentic development
sections.summary: He notes surging excitement (254% increase in agentic YC startups) but cautions that agentic benchmarks remain hard. Prototypes reach 70–80% easily, but the long tail of complex scenarios is challenging.

sections.title: Defining AI agents and the agency-effectiveness axes
sections.summary: Defines an agent as an entity that reasons, acts, communicates, and adapts. Frames agency as a continuum (citing Andrew Ng) and adds effectiveness as a second axis, warning against highly agentic but low-efficacy systems, contrasting with brittle RPA.

sections.title: Core component: tool use and function calling
sections.summary: Explains foundation models outputting function calls, enabling agents to invoke APIs in a loop. Warns against one-to-one API-to-tool mapping; too many tools per prompt causes semantic collision and accuracy loss. Recommends few, clearly scoped, human-facing-action-like tools.

sections.title: Core component: orchestration patterns
sections.summary: Recommends starting simple with chains and trees, moving to agentic loops only when chains become unwieldy. Describes cyber security triage use cases. Advocates keeping fixed business logic deterministic and external to the model, using the agent only to update validated state.

sections.title: Core component: multi-agent systems
sections.summary: Justifies multi-agent systems mainly to partition large tool sets into semantically grouped agents coordinated by a router. Notes agent-to-agent protocols are early-stage and mostly intra-team so far.

sections.title: Evaluation and test-driven agent development
sections.summary: Strongly recommends investing more in evaluation. With many hyperparameters (agents, tools, model, memory), rigorous eval sets are essential. Frames this as test-driven agent development, defining agents by expected inputs and outputs to enable automated improvement.

sections.title: Evaluation tools and automatic prompt optimization
sections.summary: Recommends open-source tools: Intel Agent for synthetic input generation, Microsoft's Pirate for red teaming/jailbreaking agents, Label Studio for building evaluation sets, and trace/textrad/dspI for automatic prompt optimization using a foundation model as judge. Encourages moving from development by anecdote to batch-level aggregate analysis for more accurate optimization steps.

sections.title: Observability
sections.summary: Uses the iceberg metaphor: generative models produce content that is hard to evaluate at scale. Recommends open telemetry integrations, detailed logs and tracing, and automated clustering and summarization of failure modes to understand and improve production systems.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.summary: Insufficient evaluation is the biggest limitation. Other pitfalls include tool issues (insufficient tools, unclear descriptions, semantic overlap causing confusion), excessive complexity from chasing bells and whistles, and a weak learning loop that makes root-cause improvement hard.

sections.title: Security, safety, and conclusion
sections.summary: From the cyber security division, stresses agentic systems are a new vulnerability class. Design for safety at every layer: use tools like Pirate, good engineering principles, tripwires, and detectors to eject to human review in critical cases. Closes with a Paul Krugman quote on productivity, expressing optimism about an upshift in individual productivity through agent design patterns.

demonstrations: Cyber security incident severity triage using tree branching orchestration and multi-hop enrichment.
Externalizing fixed business logic by exposing state-updating tools with sanitization and validation.
limitations: Agentic systems are hard to get to production-grade performance.
More tools exposed in a single prompt reduces overall accuracy due to semantic collision.
Full agentic patterns are harder to measure and optimize than chains/trees.
Agent-to-agent protocols remain early with unresolved technical and security questions.
Most successful multi-agent systems so far are built within a single coordinated team.
Generative models make production failure modes hard to observe and understand at scale.
Agentic systems represent a new class of potential vulnerability requiring safety design at every layer.
quantitativeClaims: 254% increase in Y Combinator companies describing themselves as agentic over the last three years.
Leading agentic benchmarks reach roughly the 50s, 60s, and 70s on complex multi-step tasks.
Five to ten years ago, accuracy on similar tasks was in the single digits.
Easy to reach 70–80% accuracy in prototypes; long tail is increasingly challenging.
Forthcoming O'Reilly book is ~300 pages; first seven chapters on early release.
